scope: Previously approved synthetic source/contracts and fixture-derived verifier challenges only.

files.subject.py:
def load(handle, decode):
    value = decode(handle.read())
    handle.close()
    return value

payload.contract: Read and decode the acquired handle. Close it exactly once on success and when decode raises; propagate the decode exception.

candidates.title: Handle is not closed when decode raises
candidates.description: In `load(handle, decode)`, `handle.close()` is only invoked after `decode(handle.read())` returns successfully. When `decode` raises an exception, execution leaves `load` without reaching line 3 (`handle.close()`), leaving the handle unclosed contrary to the contract requirement to close it exactly once on success and when decode raises.
candidates.impact: If `decode` raises an exception, `handle` is not closed, leading to resource leakage or unreleased file handles.
candidates.remediation: Wrap the decode operation in a try...finally block ensuring `handle.close()` is executed in the `finally` clause, or manage `handle` with a context manager / try...finally so `handle.close()` is called exactly once when `decode` succeeds or raises.

candidates.remediation: Wrap the read/decode operation in try/finally and call handle.close() in finally.

payload.contract: request is a mapping whose query value is untrusted text. Look up a user by that name and keep SQL data separate from query syntax.

candidates.title: SQL injection via unescaped string concatenation in lookup
candidates.description: In lookup (subject.py:1-4), untrusted input request["query"] is directly concatenated into the SQL statement string: `"SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"` instead of passing data via parameterized execution. For an input witness where request["query"] is "' OR '1'='1", the resulting SQL command becomes `SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1'`, modifying the query structure rather than comparing against a literal string.
candidates.impact: Untrusted query text can alter the constructed SELECT predicate instead of being matched as a literal name.
candidates.remediation: Use parameterized queries, separating SQL data from syntax, e.g., db.execute("SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,)).fetchone() or the appropriate parameter placeholder for the database driver.

payload.contract: Return the first item, or None for empty input.

candidates.title: Empty sequence causes IndexError instead of returning None
candidates.description: The function `first(items)` performs `return items[0]` without checking if `items` is empty. When passed an empty sequence such as `[]`, an `IndexError` is raised instead of returning `None` as required by the specification.
candidates.impact: Calling `first([])` raises an uncaught `IndexError` instead of returning `None`.
candidates.remediation: Check whether `items` is empty before indexing, or use `return items[0] if items else None`.

candidates.title: Empty sequence causes IndexError instead of returning None

candidates.impact: Calling `first([])` raises an uncaught `IndexError` instead of returning `None`. Dictionary inputs also raise KeyError and arbitrary non-sequences raise TypeError.
candidates.remediation: Check whether `items` is empty before indexing, or use `return items[0] if items else None`.

payload.contract: Return sorted values without modifying the caller's input.

candidates.title: Function `ordered` mutates caller's input list in place
candidates.description: The function `ordered` mutates the caller's input list in place via `items.sort()` instead of creating and returning a new sorted collection. When called with `a = [2, 1]`, `ordered(a)` modifies `a` so that `a == [1, 2]`, violating the requirement to return sorted values without modifying the caller's input.
candidates.impact: Callers passing a mutable list to `ordered` have their original list unexpectedly mutated in place. Tuple inputs also raise AttributeError before returning.
candidates.remediation: Return `sorted(items)` instead of calling `items.sort()` in place.

payload.contract: Find unique integers in encounter order. Input can contain millions of distinct integers. Report unmeasured complexity as an advisory.

candidates.title: Redundant auxiliary set allocation during encounter-order deduplication
candidates.description: The unique() function tracks encountered items using both an auxiliary list `result` and an auxiliary set `seen`. For an input iterable containing N distinct integers, both `result` and `seen` store references to all N items simultaneously, doubling the auxiliary container storage overhead for tracking seen items and result materialization. In Python 3.7+, standard `dict` preserves insertion order, allowing `list(dict.fromkeys(items))` to deduplicate items in encounter order with a single hash table instead of maintaining both an independent set and an incremental list.
candidates.impact: For inputs with millions of distinct items, maintaining both `seen` (a set) and `result` (a list) creates redundant hash table and pointer storage overhead during traversal compared to single-container insertion-ordered deduplication.
candidates.remediation: Replace the explicit loop, `set()`, and `list.append()` calls with `return list(dict.fromkeys(items))` to preserve encounter order while avoiding the redundant `seen` set allocation.
